To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) instructions can control human behavior, (b) instructions can be maintained across a range of conditions, (c) instructions can be altered in a systematic manner, and (d) schedule control is not always evident in situations of diminishing marginal returns.

(a) instructions establish control over choice behavior, (b) instructions can be used to establish optimal control, (c) instructionally controlled behavior becomes sensitive to the contingencies, and (d) the sensitivity to contingencies is not perfect
instructions can control human choice in a situation of diminishing returns and, when they do so, they reduce the sensitivity of behavior to the programmed contingencies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of instructions in the acquisition and maintenance of choice patterns in situations of diminishing marginal utility.

the role of instructions in the control of choice behavior in situations in which the optimal response is not always obvious and in which the consequences of responding are not always immediately evident.
the role of instructions in human choice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

instructions can control choice behavior in situations of diminishing return, but the degree of schedule sensitivity depends on a variety of factors, including the correspondence between the instructions and the contingencies, the variability of the contingencies, and the subjects' history with the task.
instructionally controlled behavior is not always insensitive to the contingencies, but it may not always be sensitive either.
instructions are powerful, but not infallible, determinants of choice behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, when the contingencies support the instructed behavior, the behavior can remain under instructional control.
instructions are effective in controlling choice behavior, but they may also obscure the influence of the programmed contingencies on behavior.
instructionally controlled behavior is not necessarily sensitive to schedule changes, and sensitivity is not necessarily controlled by instructions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the instructions provided to humans can influence their choices in ways that are not necessarily sensitive to the contingencies.
